# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of inner links and outer links joined by pins and rollers. Each pin sits inside a roller, and the rollers ride on the cassette and chainring teeth. Every pedal stroke moves the pins and rollers a tiny amount. Dirt, grit and sand get into the joints, act like sandpaper, and wear the pins and the inside of the links. Each joint grows slightly looser, so the distance from one pin to the next gets longer. Chain makers call this elongation. The metal does not stretch. The gap between joints grows.

Lack of lubrication speeds this up. Dry or dirty chains wear faster. Wet riding, long climbs with heavy pedaling, and frequent shifting under load also add wear.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain checker tool. Clean the chain first. Place the checker hooks into the rollers and read the scale.

- A reading of 0.5 means the chain has stretched 0.5 percent. Plan to replace the chain.
- A reading of 0.75 means the chain has stretched 0.75 percent. Replace the chain now, and check the cassette and chainring.

Without a checker, use a ruler. Measure 24 pitches of a 1/2 inch chain, which is 12 inches on a new chain. Measure from the center of one pin to the center of the pin 12 inches away. A reading of about 12.06 inches means 0.5 percent wear. A reading of about 12.09 inches means 0.75 percent wear.

## When to replace the chain

Replace the chain at 0.5 percent. Waiting longer lets the chain wear the cassette and chainring teeth, which makes a new chain more expensive to fix later. Also replace the chain if it skips under pedaling load, shifts poorly, or has a stiff or broken link.

## When to replace the cassette

Replace the cassette when it shows wear. Look for teeth that have a hooked or shark fin shape, or teeth that look pointed. Replace the cassette when the chain reads 0.75 percent or more, or when a new chain skips on the cassette under load. Installing a new chain on a worn cassette causes skipping, so replace the cassette at the same time as the chain when the cassette is worn.

## Practical notes

- Clean and lube the chain regularly. Wipe off extra lube so it does not collect grit.
- Check the chain every few hundred miles or kilometers. Many chains last around 1,500 to 3,000 miles, depending on riding conditions.
- Match chain and cassette speeds. An 11 speed chain must go on an 11 speed cassette.
- Replace the chainring when the teeth show the same hooked wear, usually after two chains on the same ring.

# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Read this whole page before you touch a bike. Work through the steps in order. If a check fails, do not return the bike to the floor. Tag it and tell the shop lead.

## Before you start

- Wear closed shoes and tie back long hair or loose clothing.
- Stand the bike in a stand or flip it upside down on a clean mat.
- Check that quick releases and axle nuts are closed or tight before you test anything.
- Never test a brake with the wheel off the bike.

## Part 1: Rim brakes

Rim brakes squeeze pads against the metal sidewall of the rim.

### 1. Look at the brake pads

- Each pad should have at least about 1 mm of rubber left above the wear line or groove.
- Pads must not be cracked, hardened, glazed, or missing chunks.
- Pads must sit flat on the rim, with the front edge slightly toe in (touching first, about 1 mm in front of the back edge).
- Pads must not touch the tire.
- A pad with grit or a shiny glaze needs cleaning with rubbing alcohol. A glazed or worn pad needs replacing.

### 2. Check the rim sidewall

- Spin the wheel and look at the braking surface. A sidewall worn to a concave dip or with a bulge is a fail. Tag the wheel.
- Look for cracks, bubbles, or a thin spot near the valve hole. Any of these is a fail.
- Check that the braking surface is clean and dry. Oil or grease on the rim is a fail until cleaned.

### 3. Check the brake pad bolts and cable

- Pull each pad by hand. It should not move or rotate in the holder.
- Check the pad bolt is tight.
- Pull the brake lever firmly. The lever should not reach the handlebar grip or bottom out.
- Squeeze the lever. Both arms should move together and reach the rim at about the same time.

### 4. Check the cable and housing

- Look for fraying, kinks, or rust on the brake cable. Any broken strand is a fail.
- Housing ends should sit firmly in their stops with no cracks.
- Cable should slide smoothly. Stiff cable needs lubricant or replacement.
- Check the cable pinch bolt is tight and the cable end cap is not missing.

### 5. Test the brake

- Lift the front wheel off the ground, spin it, and squeeze the front lever. The wheel should stop within a few turns with firm lever feel.
- Repeat for the rear wheel.
- Listen for rubbing or squealing. Light squeal from a new pad is normal. Constant rubbing is a fail.
- Check the wheel does not wobble or rub on the brake pads while spinning.

### 6. Adjust if needed

- If the pads hit the tire, adjust the pad position with the pad bolt or barrel adjuster.
- If the lever goes too far, tighten the cable at the barrel adjuster, or at the pinch bolt if the barrel is fully in.
- Test again after each change.

## Part 2: Disc brakes

Disc brakes squeeze pads against a metal rotor. Hydraulic and mechanical (cable) disc brakes are checked the same way for pads and rotors. Cable discs also need the cable check.

### 1. Check the rotor

- Spin the wheel and look at the rotor. It should run straight with no obvious wobble.
- Check for cracks, deep grooves, or blue heat marks. Any of these is a fail.
- Check the rotor bolts are tight. Use a torque wrench if the shop has one.
- Check the rotor is clean. Oil or grease on the rotor is a fail until cleaned with isopropyl alcohol.

### 2. Check the brake pads

- Look at the pad material. Each pad should have at least about 1 mm of friction material left.
- Pads must not be glazed, cracked, or contaminated with oil.
- Look for uneven wear between the two pads on one caliper. Uneven wear means the caliper may be out of line or the piston may be sticking.
- Check the pad retaining pin or clip is in place.

### 3. Check the caliper and mounting

- Check the caliper bolts are tight.
- Check the caliper sits centered over the rotor. Rubbing on one side means the caliper needs alignment.
- Check the caliper does not move when you push it sideways.
- Check the mounting tab or adapter is straight and the bolts are tight.

### 4. Check the lever and hose (hydraulic brakes)

- Squeeze the lever. It should feel firm, not spongy. Spongy feel means air in the line. Tag the bike and stop.
- Check the lever does not reach the bar grip when pulled.
- Look at the hose for cracks, bulges, leaks, or fluid around fittings. Any leak is a fail.
- Check the fluid level in the reservoir is above the minimum line.

### 4. Check the lever and cable (cable disc brakes)

- Pull the lever firmly. It should not reach the grip.
- Check the cable for fraying, kinks, or rust. Any broken strand is a fail.
- Check the cable pinch bolt is tight.

### 5. Test the brake

- Lift the wheel off the ground, spin it, and squeeze the lever. The wheel should stop firmly with a solid lever feel.
- Listen for constant rubbing or grinding. Grinding means metal on metal. Tag the bike and stop.
- Check the wheel does not wobble against the pads.

### 6. Adjust if needed

- For cable discs, use the barrel adjuster to fix lever travel. Test again.
- For hydraulic discs, do not open the hose or bleed the system unless the shop lead has trained you to do it.
- Test again after each change.

## When to tag and stop

Tag the bike, move it to the repair area, and tell the shop lead if you find any of these:

- Rim worn to a dip, bulge, or crack
- Brake pads at or below the wear line
- Rotor cracked, badly grooved, or blue
- Hydraulic lever spongy, or any fluid leak
- Cable frayed, kinked, or broken
- Brake rubs or grinds in a test spin

## Record

Write the bike ID, the brake type (rim or disc), the result (pass or fail), and your initials on the check sheet. If the shop computer is down, use paper.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of pins, rollers, and side plates. Each link pivots on pins that ride inside bushings or rollers. Every pedal stroke makes those parts rub, and grit gets in between them. Over time the pins and rollers wear, and the gap between links grows. The chain gets longer. It does not really stretch like a rubber band. The metal wears, and the pitch (the distance from one pin to the next) increases.

What speeds up wear:
- Grit and sand. Abrasive dirt acts like sandpaper inside the joints. Riding in wet, muddy, or gritty conditions is the biggest factor.
- Dry or dirty lubrication. Oil is the barrier between metal parts. Without it, metal rubs directly.
- Cross-chaining. Using the largest front ring with the largest rear cog, or the smallest with the smallest, bends the chain sharply and loads the side plates.
- Heavy pedaling and high torque. More force means more load on each pin.

A worn chain does not just wear itself out. It wears the cassette and chainrings too, because a stretched chain no longer seats properly on the teeth.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain wear indicator, often called a chain checker. It is a small tool with a hook that engages the rollers. Hook it onto the chain and see whether it drops in. Most checkers show wear as a percentage.

Without a tool, measure with a ruler:
1. Clean the chain first so grime does not skew the reading.
2. Lay a ruler or tape along the chain.
3. Measure 12 inches (30.48 cm) from the outer edge of one pin to the outer edge of the pin 12 inches away.
4. A new chain measures 12.00 inches. Check at several spots, because the wear is not always even.

Note on accuracy: a plain ruler is less precise than a checker. A ruler can show 1/16 inch of stretch at best, so it can confirm a worn chain but cannot reliably show small amounts of wear.

Wear percentage: a 12-inch section that measures 12.06 inches has stretched 0.5 percent. Common replacement guidance (check your chain and drivetrain manufacturer, since it varies):
- 0.5 percent: replace for 11 and 12 speed chains.
- 0.75 percent: replace for 9 and 10 speed chains.
- 1.0 percent: replace for 8 speed and older chains, if you still ride it.

Rule of thumb: replace the chain at 0.75 percent for most common drivetrains. Replacing early saves the cassette.

## When to replace the chain

Replace the chain when:
- It measures at or past the wear limit above.
- It skips or jumps under load, especially on the biggest cogs.
- You see stiff links, rust, or flaking plates that do not move freely. Clean and lube first, then recheck. If the stiffness returns, replace the chain.
- The chain has visible damage such as a cracked or bent plate.

If you replace a chain at around 0.5 to 0.75 percent, the cassette and chainrings usually survive. If you keep riding a chain past 1.0 percent, expect to replace the cassette and possibly the chainrings too.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette is the set of rear cogs. Its teeth wear into a hooked or shark-fin shape as the chain wears into them.

Replace the cassette when:
- The teeth look hooked or pointed when you look at them from the side.
- The new chain skips or slips under pedal pressure. This is the most common sign. A new chain on a worn cassette will jump, usually on the biggest cog or the cog you use most.
- The chain has been run past its wear limit for a long time.
- Teeth are chipped, bent, or missing.

Tip: when replacing the chain, check the cassette. If it is worn, replace both together. A new chain on an old cassette wears out quickly, and a worn chain on a new cassette will damage the new cassette.

## Quick rules
- Measure the chain every 500 to 1000 miles or every few months of regular riding.
- Replace the chain at 0.75 percent for most drivetrains.
- Replace the cassette when a new chain slips.
- Clean and lube the chain regularly. It extends the life of every part.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of pins, rollers, and side plates. Each link pivots on pins that ride inside bushings or rollers. Every pedal stroke makes those parts rub, and grit gets in between them. Over time the pins and rollers wear, and the gap between links grows. The chain gets longer. It does not really stretch like a rubber band. The metal wears, and the pitch (the distance from one pin to the next) increases.

What speeds up wear:
- Grit and sand. Abrasive dirt acts like sandpaper inside the joints. Riding in wet, muddy, or gritty conditions is the biggest factor.
- Dry or dirty lubrication. Oil is the barrier between metal parts. Without it, metal rubs directly.
- Cross-chaining. Using the largest front ring with the largest rear cog, or the smallest with the smallest, bends the chain sharply and loads the side plates.
- Heavy pedaling and high torque. More force means more load on each pin.

A worn chain does not just wear itself out. It wears the cassette and chainrings too, because a stretched chain no longer seats properly on the teeth.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain wear indicator, often called a chain checker. It is a small tool with a hook that engages the rollers. Hook it onto the chain and see whether it drops in. Most checkers show wear as a percentage.

Without a tool, measure with a ruler:
1. Clean the chain first so grime does not skew the reading.
2. Lay a ruler or tape along the chain.
3. Measure 12 inches (30.48 cm) from the outer edge of one pin to the outer edge of the pin 12 inches away.
4. A new chain measures 12.00 inches. Check at several spots, because the wear is not always even.

Note on accuracy: a plain ruler is less precise than a checker. A ruler can show 1/16 inch of stretch at best, so it can confirm a worn chain but cannot reliably show small amounts of wear.

Wear percentage: a 12-inch section that measures 12.06 inches has stretched 0.5 percent. Common replacement guidance (check your chain and drivetrain manufacturer, since it varies):
- 0.5 percent: replace for 11 and 12 speed chains.
- 0.75 percent: replace for 9 and 10 speed chains.
- 1.0 percent: replace for 8 speed and older chains, if you still ride it.

Rule of thumb: replace the chain at 0.75 percent for most common drivetrains. Replacing early saves the cassette.

## When to replace the chain

Replace the chain when:
- It measures at or past the wear limit above.
- It skips or jumps under load, especially on the biggest cogs.
- You see stiff links, rust, or flaking plates that do not move freely. Clean and lube first, then recheck. If the stiffness returns, replace the chain.
- The chain has visible damage such as a cracked or bent plate.

If you replace a chain at around 0.5 to 0.75 percent, the cassette and chainrings usually survive. If you keep riding a chain past 1.0 percent, expect to replace the cassette and possibly the chainrings too.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette is the set of rear cogs. Its teeth wear into a hooked or shark-fin shape as the chain wears into them.

Replace the cassette when:
- The teeth look hooked or pointed when you look at them from the side.
- The new chain skips or slips under pedal pressure. This is the most common sign. A new chain on a worn cassette will jump, usually on the biggest cog or the cog you use most.

## Quick rules
- Measure the chain every 500 to 1000 miles or every few months of regular riding.
- Replace the chain at 0.75 percent for most drivetrains.
- Replace the cassette when a new chain slips.
- Clean and lube the chain regularly. It extends the life of every part.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

Read all of this once before you start. Work slowly. Keep small parts like nuts and the quick release skewer in one place.

## What you need

- Tire levers (2 or 3, plastic is best)
- Patch kit: patches, tube glue, sandpaper or a rasp (called an abrader)
- Pump (hand pump or frame pump)
- Spare tube if you have one, which is faster than patching
- A wrench for the axle nuts, if your wheel has nuts instead of a quick release
- A bowl or puddle of water, or a wet hand, to find the hole
- A marker or chalk

## Step 1: Stop safely and get the wheel off

1. Move the bike to a flat, safe spot off the road.
2. Shift the rear derailleur to the smallest cog (the gear with the fewest teeth) if the rear wheel is flat. This makes the wheel easier to remove and put back.
3. Open the quick release lever on the wheel, or loosen the axle nuts with a wrench.
4. Lift the bike, remove the wheel, and set it down. On a rear wheel, lift the chain off the cog as the wheel comes out.

## Step 2: Let out the rest of the air

1. Remove the valve cap.
2. Press the small pin in the center of the valve. Air hisses out.
3. For a Presta valve (thin valve with a small lock nut on top), unscrew the top nut first, then press the pin.

## Step 3: Pull the tire off the rim

1. Push the bead (the stiff edge of the tire) on one side into the center well of the rim all the way around. This gives slack.
2. Hook the first tire lever under the bead, next to the valve hole or on the opposite side from the valve. Pull the tip up and over the rim edge.
3. Hook a second lever a few inches away, and pull it over the rim too. Keep the first lever hooked to the spokes so it stays put.
4. Use a third lever to work the next section off. Stop if the lever cannot move easily. Push the bead back into the well and try again from a different spot.
5. Once one side of the bead is off the rim, pull the tube out through the gap. Leave the valve stem in the tire if you can.

## Step 4: Find the hole

1. Put a small amount of air in the tube, just enough to round it out.
2. Listen for a hiss. Or hold the tube under water and watch for bubbles.
3. If you have no water, wipe your wet hand or spit-free damp cloth along the tube. Feel for air.
4. Mark the hole with chalk or a marker. Let all air out again.

## Step 5: Check the tire for the cause

1. Run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire. Feel for thorns, glass, wire, or sharp stones.
2. Remove anything you find. A cut that stays in the tire will puncture the new patch.
3. Check the outer tread too. Remove any stone stuck in the tread.

## Step 6: Prepare the patch area

1. Dry the area around the hole.
2. Rough the area with sandpaper or the abrader in the kit. Make a patch-sized area that looks dull and scratched, about the size of the patch.
3. Wipe away the dust with a clean finger or cloth. Do not touch the roughened area again.

## Step 7: Glue and patch

1. Squeeze out a thin layer of glue on the roughened area. Spread it lightly to the edges of the patch area. Do not use too much.
2. Wait for the glue to go tacky. This means it is dry to the touch but still a little sticky. This usually takes 1 to 3 minutes. Follow the instructions in your kit.
3. Peel the foil backing off the patch. Do not touch the sticky side.
4. Place the patch on the glue, centered over the hole.
5. Press hard with your thumb for at least 30 seconds. Press from the middle out to the edges.
6. Leave the patch in place. Do not pull it off to check.

## Step 8: Reinstall the tube

1. Add a little air to the tube, just enough to give it shape. This keeps it from folding and pinching.
2. Push the valve through the valve hole in the rim first.
3. Tuck the tube inside the tire evenly all the way around. Make sure no part of the tube is trapped under the bead.
4. Starting at the valve, push one bead back onto the rim with your thumbs. Work both ways from the valve.
5. For the last section, use the tire levers only if needed. Work slowly and keep the tube away from the lever tips. A pinched tube will fail again quickly.
6. Check the bead on both sides. You should see the tire sitting evenly in the rim with no bulge or gap.

## Step 9: Inflate and check

1. Inflate the tire a little, then look at the bead on both sides again. The tire should sit evenly with no bulge.
2. Inflate to the pressure printed on the sidewall of the tire. Use the pump gauge if you have one.
3. Use a firm hand on the tire to check for soft spots. Let the tire settle.

## Step 10: Put the wheel back on

1. Line up the wheel in the dropouts (the slots in the frame).
2. On a rear wheel, put the chain back on the smallest cog if you moved it.
3. Tighten the quick release or axle nuts. The quick release lever should leave a firm mark on your palm when closed.
4. Spin the wheel. It should turn freely and not rub on the brake pads or frame.
5. Squeeze the brake and check that the wheel stops cleanly.

## Step 11: Ride carefully

1. Ride slowly for a few minutes. Listen for rubbing.
2. Check the tire again after about 10 minutes of riding. A patch needs time to bond, so ride gently for the first few miles.
3. If the tire goes soft again, the patch or tube may need replacing. Visit the cooperative shop for a new tube.

## If it fails

- Tire goes flat again quickly: the hole may have been missed, or the patch did not bond. Find a second hole, or use a spare tube.
- Bulge on the side of the tire: the tire bead is not seated. Let air out and reseat the bead.
- Pinch flat (two small holes side by side): the tube was pinched by the rim or lever. Use a spare tube and check the rim edge for sharp spots.

## Tips

- A spare tube is faster and easier on the roadside. Patch the old tube later at home.
- Carry a pump, tire levers, and at least one spare tube on every ride.

## Step 9: Inflate and check

1. Inflate the tire a little, then look at the bead on both sides again. The tire should sit evenly with no bulge.
2. Inflate to the pressure printed on the sidewall of the tire. Use the pump gauge if you have one.
3. Use a firm hand on the tire to check for soft spots. Let the tire settle.

## Step 10: Put the wheel back on

1. Line up the wheel in the dropouts (the slots in the frame).
2. On a rear wheel, put the chain back on the smallest cog if you moved it.
3. Tighten the quick release or axle nuts. The quick release lever should leave a firm mark on your palm when closed.
4. Spin the wheel. It should turn freely and not rub on the brake pads or frame.
5. Squeeze the brake and check that the wheel stops cleanly.

## Step 11: Ride carefully

1. Ride slowly for a few minutes. Listen for rubbing.
2. Check the tire again after about 10 minutes of riding. A patch needs time to bond, so ride gently for the first few miles.
3. If the tire goes soft again, the patch or tube may need replacing. Visit the cooperative shop for a new tube.

## If it fails

- Tire goes flat again quickly: the hole may have been missed, or the patch did not bond. Find a second hole, or use a spare tube.
- Bulge on the side of the tire: the tire bead is not seated. Let air out and reseat the bead.
- Pinch flat (two small holes side by side): the tube was pinched by the rim or lever. Use a spare tube and check the rim edge for sharp spots.

- A spare tube is faster and easier on the roadside. Patch the old tube later at home.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you tighten a fastener. Most bicycle fasteners are small, and the threads are often aluminum, titanium, or carbon fiber. Hand tightening by feel can be off by a wide margin, and both directions cause failures.

- Too loose: parts slip, creep, or come off. A loose stem can let the bar rotate. A loose caliper can rub or move under braking. A loose crank bolt can damage the spindle.
- Too tight: threads strip, aluminum deforms, and the bolt can snap. Carbon parts can crack or crush, since carbon does not yield the way metal does. An over tightened bolt can also make a part impossible to remove later.
- Correct clamping force: many bike parts hold each other by friction. A bolt pulls two parts together with a set force, and that force creates the grip. The torque spec is the wrench reading that produces the right force.

Use a click type or digital torque wrench for most work. Set the value, tighten until the click, and stop. Do not keep turning after the click.

## Units

- Nm is newton meters, the usual unit on modern bike parts.
- In lb is inch pounds, found on some older or American spec parts.
- 1 Nm equals about 8.85 in lb.

## Common torque values across a bike

These are typical values from common manufacturer specs. Always use the number printed on the part or in the manufacturer manual, because values vary by brand and model. Carbon parts often have lower limits.

### Cockpit

- Stem faceplate bolts: about 5 Nm. These clamp the stem onto the steerer. Tighten them evenly in a cross pattern, a little at a time, so the faceplate closes flat.
- Stem top cap and expander bolt: about 5 to 6 Nm. Set headset preload first, then tighten the cap bolt. Over tightening can crack a carbon steerer.
- Handlebar clamp bolts (stem to bar): about 5 Nm. Carbon bars often specify 5 to 6 Nm. Too tight can crush a carbon bar, and too loose lets the bar twist under load.
- Brake and shifter lever clamp bolts: about 4 to 5 Nm on most bars. Too loose lets the lever rotate. Too tight can crack a carbon bar.

### Seat

- Seatpost clamp bolt: about 5 to 6 Nm. Too loose lets the post slip. Carbon posts and frames often specify less, so check the printed limit.
- Saddle rail clamp bolts: about 5 Nm. Keep them snug enough to hold the saddle angle under load.

### Brakes and wheels

- Rim brake caliper mounting bolt: about 6 to 8 Nm. Loose calipers shift and rub the rim.
- Disc brake caliper mounting bolts: about 6 to 8 Nm. Check that the bolt pattern and adapter match the frame.
- Six bolt disc rotor bolts: about 4 to 6 Nm. Tighten in a star pattern. Loose rotors wobble and cause pulsing.
- Centerlock rotor lockring: about 40 Nm, usually with a dedicated tool. Use the manufacturer value.
- Quick release skewers: not torqued. Close them by feel with the correct lever force, so the lever sits firmly without overclamping.
- Thru axles (front and rear): about 10 to 15 Nm, depending on the hub. Check the hub spec.

### Drivetrain

- Crank arm bolt, modern self extracting or Hollowtech style: about 35 to 50 Nm. Too loose can damage the crank interface. Too tight can damage the bolt or the crank.
- Pedal spindle into crank: about 35 Nm on most pedals. Apply grease to the threads if the manufacturer allows it. Pedals are often marked L and R, and the threads run in opposite directions.
- Chainring bolts: about 8 to 12 Nm, tightened in a star pattern. Loose rings cause shifting problems and can damage the spider.
- Cassette lockring: about 30 to 50 Nm, with a lockring tool. Loose lockrings let the cassette creep.
- Front derailleur clamp bolt: about 5 to 6 Nm. Too loose lets the derailleur rotate.
- Rear derailleur hanger bolt: about 8 to 10 Nm, or as the frame or hanger spec states. Hangers bend easily, so avoid overtightening.

### Frame and bottom bracket

- Threaded bottom bracket cups: often about 35 to 50 Nm, depending on the standard. Press fit bottom brackets have their own specs.
- Water bottle cage bolts: about 4 to 5 Nm. Carbon frames often need a low value.
- Rack and fender mounting bolts: about 4 to 5 Nm.

## Practical notes

- Thread prep: Most specs assume clean, dry threads unless the manual says to lubricate. Use grease or anti seize only where the manufacturer allows it. Lubricant can change the clamping force, so the same number can over tighten a lubricated bolt.
- Carbon parts: Use carbon assembly paste only if the manufacturer recommends it. Check the printed torque limit every time.
- Order: Set the part in place, start every bolt by hand, then tighten to the spec in a cross or star pattern when the part has several bolts.
- Calibration: Store the wrench at its lowest setting. Have it checked or calibrated on a regular schedule, since accuracy drifts with use.
- When no spec is known: Look up the part model, check the manufacturer manual, or use the lowest value in the range and check that the part holds.

## Summary

Torque specs protect both function and material. Use the printed value on the part first, use the table above as a guide, and stop at the click.

The full step-by-step guide is saved at workbench/flat-tire-patch-guide.md. The short version:

1. Remove the wheel. Shift the rear chain to the smallest cog, open the quick release, and lift the wheel out.
2. Release all air through the valve.
3. Push the tire bead to the center of the rim, then pry one side off with two tire levers.
4. Pull out the tube and find the hole by inflating it slightly and listening or feeling for air. Mark it.
5. Check the tire inside for glass or thorns.
6. Scuff a 3 cm circle around the hole, apply a thin layer of glue, wait until it is tacky, then press on the patch for 30 seconds.
7. Put the tube back in, seat the tire bead, and inflate to the pressure printed on the sidewall.

If you carry a spare tube, swapping it is faster.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative

## What you need

- Two or three tire levers (plastic is safest for the rim)
- Tube patch kit: patches, glue, and a sandpaper scuffer
- Hand pump or CO2 inflator
- Spare tube, if you carry one (fastest fix)
- Marker or chalk
- Multitool with Allen keys, for wheel removal if needed
- A dollar bill or tire boot for a cut in the tire wall

## Step 1: Secure the bike and remove the wheel

1. Turn the bike upright and stand it against something, or flip it onto the saddle and handlebars.
2. Rear wheel: shift the chain onto the smallest rear cog. Open the quick release lever, or loosen the axle nuts. Pull the rear derailleur back gently and lift the wheel out of the frame.
3. Front wheel: open the quick release and lift the wheel out of the fork.
4. If the brake is in the way, open the brake quick release or squeeze the brake lever and slide the wheel out.

## Step 2: Let out all the air

1. Remove the cap on the valve.
2. Presta valve (thin, with a small top nut): unscrew the top nut, then press the pin to release air.
3. Schrader valve (fat, like a car tire): press the pin in the center with a fingernail or key.

## Step 3: Remove one side of the tire

1. Push the tire bead (the edge that sits on the rim) into the center of the rim all the way around. This gives you slack.
2. Hook the first tire lever under the bead at a spot away from the valve.
3. Hook the lever onto a spoke so it stays in place.
4. Insert a second lever a hand width away and pry the bead up over the rim.
5. Slide the second lever around the rim to pop the bead free. Stop if you feel resistance and push the bead back toward the center.
6. Once one side is off, pull the tube out of the tire. Carefully ease the valve out of the rim hole.

## Step 4: Find the hole

1. Inflate the tube a little, just enough to see its shape.
2. Listen for air leaking, or run the tube slowly past your cheek or wet fingers.
3. Bubbles in water (a puddle or water bottle) show the hole clearly.
4. Mark the hole with a marker or chalk.
5. Check inside the tire. Run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire. Remove any glass, thorns, or wire. Leaving these in place will puncture the new tube.
6. Look at the rim. If the rim tape has a hole or the spoke ends stick through, a tube can pinch or bulge. Cover any sharp spoke ends with tape or a folded patch.

## Step 5: Patch the tube

1. Let the tube deflate fully again.
2. Dry the area around the mark. Dirt or oil stops the glue from sticking.
3. Use the sandpaper scuffer to roughen a circle about 3 cm across around the hole. Do not scrape off too much rubber.
4. Wipe away the dust with a clean finger or cloth.
5. Spread a thin, even layer of glue over the roughened area. Use just enough to cover the area, not a thick puddle.
6. Wait until the glue is tacky. It should look dull and feel slightly sticky, not wet. This usually takes 1 to 3 minutes. Follow the time on your patch kit.
7. Peel the foil backing off the patch. Do not touch the sticky side with your fingers.
8. Center the patch over the hole and press firmly. Hold for 30 seconds or more. Press from the middle toward the edges to push out air bubbles.
9. If the patch kit says to wait before riding, wait for the full time.

1. Inflate the tube slightly so it has a round shape. This prevents it from folding inside the tire.
2. Put the valve through the rim hole first.
3. Tuck the tube evenly inside the tire, starting at the valve and working both directions. Keep the tube from twisting.
4. Check that the tube is not sticking out between the tire and rim anywhere.
5. Push the tire bead back onto the rim with your thumbs, starting opposite the valve and working toward it. The last section near the valve is the hardest.
6. If the last section is tight, use a lever with care. Never pry hard on the tube. This is the most common way to pinch and puncture a new tube.
7. Check the bead. Both edges of the tire should sit evenly in the rim channel on both sides. Gently push the valve straight so it sits at a right angle to the rim.

1. Inflate with the pump until the tire feels firm. The correct pressure is printed on the tire sidewall. Stop at a level you can ride on if you are unsure.
2. Spin the tire and watch the sides for wobble or bulge.
3. Look at the tire bead again. If the tire bulges on one side, let the air out and reseat that section.
4. Wait a few minutes and check the pressure again. A good patch holds air.

1. Front wheel: set the wheel into the fork, center it, and close the quick release firmly.

- Use the spare tube if you have one. It is faster and avoids a second patch.

- A cut in the tire wall: place a dollar bill or tire boot inside the tire over the cut so the tube does not bulge through.

- Do not ride with the tire at low pressure. Pinch flats happen fast.

# Winter Storage Routine

Cleaning
Before storing a bike for the winter, wash off road salt, grit, and grime. Use warm water with a mild dish soap and a soft brush, then rinse with a hose on low pressure and keep water away from the bottom bracket, hubs, and headset bearings. Dry every surface with a clean rag. Wipe the drivetrain with a degreaser and a stiff brush, working through the chain, cassette, and chainrings until the parts look clean. Clean the brake rotors or rims with rubbing alcohol so no oil or dirt remains on the braking surface.

Lubrication
Once the drivetrain is clean and dry, apply a fresh coat of chain lube. Run the chain through your fingers while you turn the cranks backward so the lube reaches every roller. Wipe off the excess with a clean rag, since surplus lube attracts dust over the winter. Put a light coat of grease on the seatpost, the saddle rails, and any threaded fasteners that could seize, such as pedal threads and stem bolts. Add a drop of light oil to the derailleur pivots and cable ends. Keep lube away from the brake pads and rotors.

Tires
Check tire pressure and inflate each tire to a little below its maximum rated pressure. Low pressure protects the tire from damage, and rim rubber stays flexible. Inspect the tread and sidewalls for cuts, embedded glass, and cracks, and replace any tire that shows damage. If the bike will sit for several months, hang it off the ground so no tire carries its weight, or set it on a stand. Storing tires in a cool, dark place out of direct sunlight also slows the aging of the rubber.

Where to Keep the Bike
Store the bike indoors in a dry place where the temperature stays above freezing and does not swing widely. A basement, a closet, or a corner of the garage away from exterior walls works well. Avoid damp areas, because moisture causes rust on chains, cables, and bolts. Keep the bike away from fuel, paint, and chemicals, and keep it out of direct sunlight, which fades and dries out rubber parts. Hang the bike from a wall hook or set it on a stand, and check on it once a month for rust, dry seals, and flat tires.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide covers a full tube repair with a patch kit, from removing the wheel to checking the repair. Work somewhere safe off the road.

## What you need

- Tire levers (2 or 3)
- Patch kit: sandpaper or scuffer, rubber cement, patches
- Tire pump or CO2 inflator
- A bowl of water, or a way to listen for air leaks
- Chalk or a pen to mark the leak
- Your spare tube, if the patch kit fails

## Step 1: Find the flat

1. Check the tire for the cause, such as glass, a nail, or a thorn. Remove it with pliers if it is still in the tire.
2. Note the position of any object so you can find the hole.

## Step 2: Remove the wheel

1. Shift the chain to the smallest rear cog and the smallest front ring. This gives slack.
2. Rear wheel: lift the derailleur back, pull the wheel out of the dropouts, and lift the chain off the cog if needed.
3. Front wheel: open the quick release lever or loosen the axle nuts, then pull the wheel out.
4. Do not press the brake lever while the wheel is out, unless you are using a removable brake pad setup.

## Step 3: Deflate the tube

1. Unscrew the valve cap and the lock nut on a Presta valve.
2. Press the valve core to let the air out. Squeeze the tire to push out the rest.

## Step 4: Remove the tire

# Chain and cassette wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of pins, rollers, and inner and outer link plates. The pins sit inside bushings in the link plates. Each pedal stroke loads these pins, and each link bends around the front and rear sprockets. Friction between the pins and bushings slowly wears a little metal away from both parts.

Dirt and grit speed this up. Sand and grime act like a fine abrasive inside the joints. Dry or dirty chains wear much faster than clean, lubricated ones.

The chain does not stretch like rubber. The metal parts wear, the gap between pins grows, and each link becomes slightly longer. That lengthening is called chain elongation.

## How to measure chain wear

The standard tool is a chain checker. Hook the checker's pin into a roller, then check whether the other end of the tool drops into the chain's pitch. Use the tool's marked scale to read the wear percentage. Test at two or three spots along the chain, because wear is uneven.

Without a checker, use a ruler:

1. Lay the chain flat and hold it taut.
2. Measure from the center of one pin to the center of the pin 12 inches (305 mm) away. A new chain measures 12.00 inches, because the pitch of a 10 or 11 speed chain is 0.5 inch (12.7 mm), and 24 pitches make 12 inches.
3. Divide the extra length by 12 inches to get the percentage of wear.

At 0.5 percent, the chain measures about 12.06 inches. At 0.75 percent, it measures about 12.09 inches. A ruler is less precise than a checker, so be careful reading the small difference.

## When to replace the chain

- Replace the chain at 0.5 to 0.75 percent elongation. Many shops replace at 0.5 percent on 10 and 11 speed chains, and 0.75 percent is the usual upper limit.
- Replace it sooner if you see rust, stiff links that will not flex, or a bent or damaged plate.
- Replace it if the rear gears skip or the chain jumps under load, even when the measurement is still within the limit.

If you wait far past the limit, the cassette and front chainrings wear quickly, and a new chain may no longer fit the worn teeth.

## Why chain wear damages the cassette

A new chain sits deep between the cassette teeth. A worn chain sits higher, because its pitch is longer than the cassette teeth expect. Each stroke then pushes the chain against the tooth faces and wears them. Over time, the teeth take on a hooked or shark fin shape. A hooked tooth catches the chain and lets it skip.

## How to check the cassette

1. Look at the teeth from the side. Healthy teeth are symmetrical and pointed the same way as the cassette.
2. Look for hooked or shark fin teeth, where the tooth tip is sharp and leans forward.
3. Check whether the chain rides high on the teeth or skips under pedaling load.
4. Check for missing or broken teeth.

## When to replace the cassette

- Replace the cassette when the teeth are hooked, shark fin shaped, or worn to a point.
- Replace it when the chain skips under load, even with a new chain.
- Replace it when a tooth is broken or missing.
- Do not put a new chain on a worn cassette for long. The new chain will wear quickly on the old teeth and may skip.

As a general rule, replace the chain and the cassette together when the cassette is worn. Replace only the chain when the chain is worn and the cassette still has healthy teeth.

## Practical notes

- Clean and lubricate the chain regularly, especially after wet rides.
- Measure the chain every few hundred miles or kilometers, or on a fixed schedule.
- A 10 speed cassette and an 11 speed chain are not interchangeable. Match the chain to the cassette speed count.

# Week Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack and why. Pack the bike items first, then clothing, then camp or lodging gear, then tools and documents.

## Bike and repair kit
- Spare inner tubes, two or three, matched to your tire size. Flats are the most common roadside failure, and a spare takes minutes to fit.
- Tire levers, two or three. Needed to remove a tire from the rim.
- Mini pump or CO2 inflator with cartridges. A pump gets you moving after a flat. Check that the valve type matches your tubes.
- Patch kit. Fixes a tube that has a small puncture and saves a spare.
- Multi-tool with chain breaker and the hex and Torx sizes your bike uses. Covers most adjustments.
- Spoke wrench, if you ride wheels with spokes that loosen on rough roads.
- Chain quick link matched to your chain speed. A broken chain cannot be ridden home without one.
- Small bottle of chain lube. A dry chain wears fast and shifts poorly.
- Brake pads, spare set, if your brakes wear fast on the route. Replace worn pads before the tour.
- Derailleur hanger spare, if your frame uses a replaceable hanger. A bent hanger ends a day.
- Cable and housing spare, only if you have a brake or shift cable that wears often.
- Rag or two and a small bottle of degreaser. Keeps hands and drivetrain clean.

## Safety and visibility
- Helmet. Required for most tours and protects against falls.
- Front light and rear light, with spare batteries or a charging cable. Needed for dusk, tunnels, and fog.
- Reflective vest or clothing. Makes you visible to drivers in low light.
- Bell or horn. Warns walkers and other riders.

## Clothing
- Cycling shorts, three or four pairs. The padded liner prevents saddle sores on long days and makes laundry a choice.
- Jerseys, three or four. Moisture wicking fabric dries overnight.
- Base layers, one or two. Keep warm in cool mornings and evenings.
- Light insulated jacket. Covers cool descents and chilly evenings.
- Rain jacket and rain pants. Protect you on wet days and keep wind off.
- Gloves, full finger for cold mornings and a light pair for warm days. Protect hands in a fall and cut vibration.
- Socks, four to five pairs. Wool blends resist odor and dry faster.
- Casual clothes for evenings, one set. Lets you rest in street clothes.
- Sleepwear and underwear, enough for the week. Pack a few spares in case of a wet day.
- Sun hat or cycling cap and sunglasses. Reduce glare and sun exposure.
- Walking shoes or sandals, optional. Give your feet a rest from cycling shoes.

## Sleep and camp gear
Use this section only if you are camping. Skip it for hotel stays.
- Tent or bivy, with stakes and a repair kit.
- Sleeping bag rated for the coldest night you expect.
- Sleeping pad. Insulates from the ground and adds comfort.
- Pillow, inflatable or stuff sack with clothes. Improves sleep after long days.

## Food and hydration
- Water bottles, two or three, with cages on the bike. Dehydration reduces speed and focus quickly.
- Water filter or purification tablets, if water sources are uncertain.
- Snacks that travel well, such as nuts, bars, and dried fruit. Keep energy steady between stops.
- Small stove and fuel, only if you cook on the road.

## Toiletries and health
- Sunscreen, with a high SPF. Protects skin on long rides.
- Lip balm with SPF.
- Chamois cream. Reduces friction on long days in the saddle.
- Basic first aid kit: bandages, antiseptic, blister pads, pain relievers, and any personal medication.
- Hand sanitizer and toilet paper. Useful at rest stops that lack supplies.
- Insect repellent, if you ride in mosquito areas.

## Documents and money
- ID, passport if needed, and insurance cards. Required for hotel check in and for care after a crash.
- Cash and a card. Some rural stops take only cash.
- Printed route map and emergency contacts. Phones fail or lose signal.
- Bike insurance or receipt, if you need it for claims.

## Electronics
- Phone with a mount for navigation. Keep it charged.
- Power bank and charging cables. Covers the nights without an outlet.
- Camera or action camera, optional.

## Packing tips
- Pack heavy items low and close to the bike center of gravity.
- Use dry bags or waterproof stuff sacks for clothing and electronics.
- Keep tools and the repair kit in an easy reach bag.
- Weigh the total load. Aim for the lightest kit you can use every day.

# Week Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack and why. Pack the bike items first, then clothing, then camp or lodging gear, then tools and documents.

## Bike and repair kit
- Spare inner tubes, two or three, matched to your tire size. Flats are the most common roadside failure, and a spare takes minutes to fit.
- Tire levers, two or three. Needed to remove a tire from the rim.
- Mini pump or CO2 inflator with cartridges. A pump gets you moving after a flat. Check that the valve type matches your tubes.
- Patch kit. Fixes a tube that has a small puncture and saves a spare.
- Multi-tool with chain breaker and the hex and Torx sizes your bike uses. Covers most adjustments.
- Spoke wrench, if you ride wheels with spokes that loosen on rough roads.
- Chain quick link matched to your chain speed. A broken chain cannot be ridden home without one.
- Small bottle of chain lube. A dry chain wears fast and shifts poorly.
- Brake pads, spare set, if your brakes wear fast on the route. Replace worn pads before the tour.
- Derailleur hanger spare, if your frame uses a replaceable hanger. A bent hanger ends a day.
- Cable and housing spare, only if you have a brake or shift cable that wears often.
- Rag or two and a small bottle of degreaser. Keeps hands and drivetrain clean.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide covers a standard clincher bike tire with a patch kit. Read each step fully before you start it.

## What you need

- Patch kit (glue or self-adhesive patches, sandpaper or a scuffer, and a foil or chalk marker)
- Two or three tire levers (plastic levers are best; a flat screwdriver works in a pinch)
- A hand pump or CO2 inflator
- A small bowl of water, or a wet cloth, to find leaks
- A marker or pen
- A 15 mm wrench if your wheel has nuts instead of a quick release

## Step 1: Pick a safe spot and set up the bike

Move the bike off the road and onto flat ground. Shift the rear derailleur to the smallest cog, which is the one with the most teeth, so the chain sits on the smallest gear. Turn the bike upside down on its seat and handlebars, or prop it against a fence or tree.

## Step 2: Remove the wheel

For a quick release, flip the lever open. Turn the nut on the other side of the axle counterclockwise a few turns so it can slide off. If the wheel has nuts, use the wrench to loosen both nuts.

If the bike has rim brakes, open the brake quick release on the brake arm so the tire clears the pads. If the bike has disc brakes, do not squeeze the brake lever while the wheel is out, because that can push the pads together.

Lift the wheel out. Keep the rear wheel's chain side away from your hands.

## Step 3: Let the air out

Find the valve. There are two types:

- **Presta** (thin valve with a small nut at the top): unscrew the small nut first, then press the tip at the top of the valve to release air.
- **Schrader** (thick valve like a car tire): press the pin in the center of the valve with your thumbnail or the back of a key.

Squeeze the tire all the way around to push out the remaining air.

## Step 4: Take the tire off the rim

1. Push one side of the tire bead (the tire edge that sits in the rim) toward the center of the rim, all the way around. This gives you slack.
2. Start next to the valve. Slide one tire lever under the bead, then hook the lever over a spoke. This keeps the lever in place.
3. Slide a second lever under the bead about 3 to 4 inches away, and pry the bead up over the rim edge.
4. Keep going with a third lever if needed, moving around the wheel. Do not use a lever to pull the tire all the way off at once.
5. Once one side is off the rim, pull the valve out of the rim hole, then pull the tube out from inside the tire.

Do not use metal screwdrivers on the rim. They can scratch it and damage the tube.

## Step 5: Find the hole

1. Put a small amount of air into the tube. Just enough to shape it.
2. Listen for a hiss, or feel along the tube with your fingers. Slowly move the tube through the bowl of water or drag a wet cloth along it. Bubbles mark the hole.
3. Use a marker to circle the hole. Let the tube dry if you used water.
4. Deflate the tube again.

If you find more than one hole, or a hole longer than about 1 inch, or a tear near the valve, the tube is best replaced. Patches on tears often fail.

## Step 6: Check the tire for the cause

Run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire. Look for glass, thorns, wire, or sharp stones. Remove anything you find. A piece left inside will puncture the new tube again.

If the object went through the tire, a tire boot (a small patch placed inside the tire) can help. Otherwise, the tire should be replaced soon.

## Step 7: Prepare the patch area

1. Use the sandpaper or scuffer from the kit to rough the area around the hole. Cover a circle about 1 inch wider than the patch.
2. Brush away any dust with your fingers or a clean cloth. Do not touch the roughed area with your fingers again, because skin oil weakens the glue.

## Step 8: Apply glue and patch (glue kits)

1. Squeeze a thin, even layer of glue onto the roughed area. Do not make it thick.
2. Wait until the glue is tacky. Touch it lightly with a clean fingertip or the corner of the foil. It should feel sticky but not wet. This often takes 1 to 3 minutes. Follow the kit instructions for the exact time.
3. Peel the foil off the patch. Do not touch the sticky side.
4. Place the patch centered over the hole.
5. Press firmly from the center outward for 30 to 60 seconds. Make sure the edges stick all the way around.
6. Leave the glue to cure for the time the kit says, usually a few minutes. Do not inflate early.

## Step 8 alternative: Self-adhesive patches

1. Clean and dry the area around the hole. Scuff it if the kit says to.
2. Peel the backing off the patch.
3. Center it over the hole and press firmly for 30 seconds, working from the center out.

## Step 9: Check the patch

Put a little air in the tube, enough to give it shape. Dip the patched area in water and look for bubbles. If the patch leaks, let it dry, deflate it, and patch again on a fresh area, or replace the tube.

## Step 10: Put the tube back in the tire

1. Deflate the tube fully and dust it lightly with talc if you have some. This keeps the tube from sticking to the tire.
2. Put the tube back into the tire, starting with the valve. Feed the valve through the rim hole first.
3. Tuck the tube evenly inside the tire all the way around. Make sure no part of the tube is trapped between the tire and the rim.
4. Put a little air in the tube, just enough to round it out. This keeps it from pinching during reinstall.

## Step 11: Put the tire back on the rim

1. Push the bead on one side back onto the rim, starting at the valve side and working away from the valve in both directions. Use your thumbs first. Use a lever only if the tire is stiff, and keep the lever away from the tube.
2. Work the last section by hand. Starting from the side opposite the valve, push the bead toward the valve and keep the last few inches as loose as possible.
3. Push the valve gently to make sure it sits straight in the rim hole.
4. Check the tire all the way around. The bead should sit evenly in the rim on both sides, with no tube showing at the edge.

## Step 12: Inflate

1. Check the pressure printed on the tire sidewall.
2. For Presta valves, unscrew the small nut at the top before pumping, then tighten it again after.
3. Pump slowly. Stop when the tire is firm enough to ride.
4. Check that the bead stays even on both sides of the rim. Bulging or a line of tube at the edge means the tire is not seated correctly. Deflate and fix it.

1. Hold the wheel in the frame with the axle fully seated in the dropouts (the slots at the frame).

3. For nuts, tighten both evenly.

5. Squeeze the brakes and check that they stop the wheel firmly.

- A patch is a repair, not a permanent fix. Carry a spare tube if you can.
- Ride gently for a few minutes after the repair, and check the pressure again soon.
- If the patch leaks, the tube is worn out. Replace it.
- Clean out the tire again if you find debris, because a hidden piece can cause another flat within a few miles.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you turn a fastener. Bicycle fasteners are tightened to a specific clamping force, and that force is set by the torque value in newton metres (Nm). Hand feel alone cannot tell you whether a bolt is at the right force.

Too loose:
- Parts slip or rotate. A loose stem can twist the bars out of line. A loose seatpost can drop under load.
- Clamps and pedals can work loose while riding, which can cause a crash.

Too tight:
- Aluminium and steel threads strip, and removal becomes hard.
- Carbon fibre parts crack or crush. Carbon clamps are the most sensitive.
- Threads and parts deform, which makes the joint weaker and harder to service.

A torque wrench keeps each bolt in the window the manufacturer designed for.

## Types of torque wrench

- Click type: you set a value, pull until the wrench clicks, then stop. This is the most common type for bikes.
- Beam type: a pointer moves along a scale. It is simple and accurate, but you must read the scale at eye level.
- Digital type: shows the reading on a screen and often beeps at the target value. Check the battery before a job.

For bikes, a click wrench in a range of about 2 to 15 Nm covers most fasteners. A separate wrench for crank and cassette work, up to about 50 Nm, is useful.

Use the correct direction. Click wrenches should be turned in the direction of the clicking arrow only. Do not hold the wrench at the set value for long periods. Store it at its lowest setting so the spring is not kept under tension.

## Common torque values

These are typical ranges. Always check the number stamped on the part and the manufacturer manual first. Where a part's marking differs from this list, follow the marking.

| Location | Typical torque (Nm) | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts (steerer clamp) | 5 to 6 | Holds the stem on the steerer. Too loose lets the bars move. Too tight can crush or crack a carbon steerer. |
| Handlebar clamp bolts (stem) | 5 to 6 | Holds the bars in place. Carbon bars need the lower end of the range. |
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 7 | Holds the saddle height. Carbon seatposts are sensitive and often marked with a maximum value. |
| Saddle rail clamp | 5 to 7 | Holds the saddle angle and position. |
| Brake lever clamp | 4 to 5 | Holds the lever on the bar. Too tight can crack carbon bars. |
| Brake caliper mounting bolts | 6 to 8 | Holds the caliper square to the rotor. Loose calipers rub and lose braking. |
| Six bolt disc rotor | 2.5 to 4 | Holds the rotor on the hub. Use a star pattern across all bolts. |
| Centre lock rotor lockring | About 40 | Holds the rotor with a single ring. Use the specific lockring tool. |
| Crank bolt (Hollowtech or square taper) | 35 to 50 | Holds the crank on the axle. Loose cranks damage the spindle and the crank interface. |
| Pedals into crank | 30 to 35 | Pedal threads are soft in aluminium cranks. Apply grease only if the manual allows. Right pedal is right hand thread, left pedal is left hand thread. |
| Bottom bracket cups or lockring | 35 to 50 | Holds the bearing cups in the frame. Check the bottom bracket type. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 | Holds the cassette on the freehub. Loose cassettes click or slip under pedalling. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 | Holds the chainrings to the crank arms. Use the crank marking as a guide. |
| Derailleur hanger bolt | 8 to 10 | Holds the rear derailleur on the frame. A loose hanger changes shifting. |
| Derailleur pulley bolt | 4 to 5 | Small fastener on the derailleur cage. Overtightening strips threads. |
| Shifter clamp bolt | 2 to 4 | Holds the shifter on the bar. Carbon bars need care. |
| Water bottle cage bolts | 4 to 5 | Holds the cage. Overtightening cracks carbon frames. |
| Thru axle (front or rear) | 15 to 20 | Holds the wheel in the dropouts. Loose axles can let the wheel shift. |
| Quick release skewer | Not torqued | Set by the lever tension, not a torque wrench. |

## Practical tips

- Clean and dry threads before fitting. Grease or anti seize only when the manual says so. Lubricants change the torque reading.
- Use thread lock only where the manual calls for it, and use the type it specifies.
- For multi bolt parts such as rotors, caliper mounts, and stem faceplates, tighten in a cross or star pattern in two steps: snug, then final torque.
- Carbon parts need a torque wrench, not an estimate. Confirm the maximum torque on the part.
- Check that the wrench is calibrated. Many shops recalibrate every year or after heavy use.
- Conversion: 1 Nm equals about 8.85 inch pounds. Some older manuals use inch pounds.

## Safety note

If a value is missing, unclear, or the part has no marking, do not guess. Check the manufacturer documentation or contact the manufacturer.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative, class handout

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of pins, bushings, and rollers joined by side plates. Each time you pedal, the pins and bushings rub against each other under load. Grit from the road gets into those joints, and lube washes out. The metal wears a little at each contact point, so the gap between pins grows. The chain gets longer. It does not stretch like rubber. The pitch, which is the distance from one pin to the next, slowly increases.

A worn chain no longer seats properly in the cassette teeth. It can skip under load, especially on the biggest cog at the back. The cassette teeth then wear to match the stretched chain, which is why a worn cassette and a worn chain tend to go together.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain checker tool. Hook the tool onto the chain. If the indicator shows 0.5, the chain has early wear. If it shows 0.75, the chain is worn and should be replaced soon. If it shows 1.0, the chain is worn out.

No tool? Use a ruler. Measure from the center of one pin to the center of the pin 12 links later. A new chain measures 12.00 inches, which is 304.8 mm. These readings mean:

* About 12.06 inches (0.5 percent stretch): early wear, keep checking.
* About 12.09 inches (0.75 percent stretch): replace the chain soon.
* About 12.12 inches (1.0 percent stretch): replace the chain now.

Check several spots around the chain, because wear is not even. Measure with the chain under light tension and clean of heavy grease.

## When to replace the chain

* Replace at 0.75 percent. Waiting longer usually damages the cassette.
* Replace sooner if the chain skips under load, makes new noise, or jumps gears.
* A rough guide is every 2,000 to 3,000 miles, but riding conditions change this a lot. Wet, gritty, or muddy riding wears chains faster. Measure instead of counting miles.
* Chains on 11 speed drivetrains are narrower than older chains, so they wear faster. Check them more often.

## When to replace the cassette

* Check the cassette teeth. Hooked or shark fin shaped teeth mean the cassette is worn.
* Replace the cassette if the chain skips on the cogs under load, even after a new chain is fitted.
* Replacing a worn chain before it reaches 0.75 percent usually saves the cassette.
* If the cassette is worn, fit a new chain at the same time. A new chain on a worn cassette will skip.

## Quick rules for the class

1. Measure the chain every few rides.
2. Replace the chain at 0.75 percent.
3. Replace the cassette only when its teeth are hooked or the chain still skips with a new chain.
4. Replace the chain and cassette as a pair when the cassette is worn.
5. Keep the chain clean and lubricated.

* About 12.12 inches (1.0 percent stretch): replace the chain now.

* Chains on 11 speed drivetrains are narrower than older chains, so they wear faster. Check them more often.

* Replace the cassette if the chain skips on the cogs under load, even after a new chain is fitted.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard you turn a fastener. Bicycle bolts are small, and many are made from aluminum or carbon fiber. Hand feel alone cannot tell you whether a bolt is at the right clamping force.

Too loose and the part can slip, loosen, rattle, or fall off while riding. A stem that twists under load or a crank that works loose can cause a crash.

Too tight and the part can fail in other ways. Threads strip, aluminum deforms, and carbon fiber cracks, often with no visible sign until the part breaks.

The manufacturer's torque value sets the clamping force the part was designed for. A torque wrench lets you reach that value every time.

## Using the wrench correctly

- Set the wrench to the target value before you start. Use Nm for most bike specs.
- Pull smoothly until the wrench clicks or the needle reaches the value. Do not jerk the handle.
- Stop at the click. Do not keep turning.
- Store the wrench at its lowest setting so the spring stays accurate.
- Use a torque wrench with a reliable calibration, and check it periodically.
- Apply the lubricant or assembly compound the manufacturer specifies. Some pastes change friction, so the same number on the wrench can produce a different clamping force.
- Conversion: 1 Nm equals about 8.85 in-lb.

## Common torque values across a bike

These are typical ranges. Always check the value printed on the part or in the manufacturer's manual, especially on carbon parts. Where a range is given, use the manufacturer's number if it differs.

### Cockpit (handlebar and stem)

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts | 5 to 6 Nm | Clamps the steerer. Too loose and the stem slips. Too tight and carbon steerers or stems can crack. |
| Handlebar clamp bolts | 4 to 6 Nm | Holds the bar in the stem. Overtightening can crush or crack carbon bars. |
| Brake lever clamp (drop bar or flat bar) | 4 to 6 Nm | Keeps the lever from rotating under braking. |
| Shifter or bar-end clamp | 4 to 5 Nm | Prevents the shifter rotating on the bar. |
| Stem expander bolt (quill stem) | about 5 to 6 Nm | Expands the stem inside the steerer. Follow the stem's marking. |

### Seatpost and saddle

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Seatpost clamp bolt | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the post in the frame. Carbon posts often need a lower value, so check the marking. |
| Saddle rail clamp | 5 to 6 Nm | Holds the saddle rails in the post head. Too loose and the saddle tilts. |

### Wheels and brakes

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Caliper mounting bolts (disc, flat mount or post mount) | 6 to 8 Nm | Keeps the caliper square to the rotor. Loose bolts can cause brake rub or sudden loss of braking. |
| Rotor bolts (6-bolt) | about 2.5 to 6 Nm, varies by maker | Holds the rotor to the hub. Use the rotor or hub manufacturer's value. |
| Center lock rotor ring | about 40 Nm (check maker) | Locks the rotor to the hub. Loose rings let the rotor wobble. |
| Thru-axle (front or rear) | about 8 to 15 Nm, varies by axle | Clamps the wheel in the frame. Loose axles can let the wheel shift or come out. |
| Cassette lockring | about 30 to 50 Nm | Holds the cassette on the freehub. Loose lockrings let the cassette creep and damage the freehub. |

### Drivetrain

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Bottom bracket (threaded, BSA) | about 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the bearing cups in the frame. Too loose and the bracket creaks or loosens. |
| Crank bolt (Hollowtech or similar) | about 35 to 55 Nm | Clamps the crank to the spindle. Loose cranks can damage the spindle and the crank. |
| Chainring bolts | about 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the rings to the spider. Loose rings can shift and drop chains. |
| Front derailleur clamp | about 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the derailleur on the seat tube. Too loose and the shifting drifts. |
| Rear derailleur hanger bolt | about 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the frame or hanger. Loose bolts can bend the hanger. |

### Pedals and other

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Pedals | about 30 to 35 Nm | Holds the pedal in the crank thread. Right pedal is a standard thread. Left pedal is a reverse thread. Loose pedals can strip threads in the crank. |
| Bottle cage bolts | about 4 to 5 Nm on metal, lower on carbon | Holds the cage to the frame boss. Overtightening can crack carbon frames. |

## Notes

- These values come from common bike maker guidance. Your bike may differ. Check the specific part and the manufacturer's manual before tightening.
- Carbon parts are the most sensitive. When in doubt, use the lower end of the range or the manufacturer's stated value.

**Both brake types:** Spin each wheel and check it sits fully in the dropouts. Squeeze each lever. It must stop well short of the bar and not sink.

**Rim brakes:** Pads hit the braking track, front edge touching first. Replace cracked, glazed, or worn pads. Check the rim for bulges, cracks, or worn grooves. Confirm the rim clears both pads when spun.

**Disc brakes:** Check rotor for bends and minimum thickness. Clean with isopropyl alcohol only. Replace pads at 1 mm or less. Re-center the caliper, then test the lever.

**Tag and tell a lead:** rim crack or bulge, bent rotor, any fluid leak, lever to the bar, snapped cable.

# Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Read this before your first shift. If a step is unclear, ask a shop lead before you work on a customer bike.

## Part 1: Setup (both brake types)

1. Stand the bike on a repair stand, or turn it upside down on a clean surface.
2. Spin each wheel by hand. Listen and look for rubbing, wobble, or a loose sound.
3. Check that each wheel sits fully in the dropouts. Check that the quick release lever or thru axle is tight.
4. Squeeze each brake lever firmly. The lever should stop well short of the handlebar. Hold it for 10 seconds. If it slowly sinks toward the bar, the brake is leaking or the cable is stretched.

## Part 2: Rim brakes

Check each item in order.

1. Pad position. The pad should hit the braking track of the rim, not the tire and not the rim edge. Set the front edge of each pad about 1 mm closer to the rim than the back edge, so the front touches first. This is called toe in.
2. Pad condition. Replace pads that are cracked, hardened, glazed (shiny), or that have a grit or metal bit stuck in them. Replace pads when the wear groove is gone.
3. Rim condition. Look along the braking track for a groove worn into the side, a bulge, a crack, or a hole near a spoke. Check the wear indicator groove if the rim has one. A rim with a crack or a bulge is not safe to ride. Tag it and tell a lead.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack for a seven-day bike tour, with the reason for each item. Pack the bike-specific gear first, then clothing, then the rest. Weigh your loaded panniers before you leave, and aim to keep the total luggage near 15 kg (about 33 lb) or less.

## 1. Bike and safety

- Helmet. Protects your head in a fall or collision. Replace it if it has taken a hard hit.
- Lights, front and rear, plus spare batteries or a USB charger. Tours often include early starts, late arrivals, and tunnels or shaded roads.
- Bike lock with key or code. Needed for stops in towns, cafes, and campsites.
- Water bottles or a hydration bladder, two or more. Carry at least 1 liter per hour of riding in warm weather.
- Saddle bag or top tube bag with a multi-tool, tire levers, and a spare tube or two. Flats are the most common roadside problem.
- Tire pump or CO2 inflator with a spare cartridge. Confirm the valve type on your tires (Presta or Schrader) so the pump fits.
- Patch kit and spare spoke or derailleur hanger if your bike uses one. A bent hanger can end a trip, so carry the spare in your bag.
- Chain lube in a small bottle. Dry or dirty chains wear fast and skip under load.
- Chain tool, quick links, and a cassette or freewheel tool if your bike needs one.
- Reflective strips or a vest for riding in traffic or at dusk.
- Bike gloves. Protect your hands in a fall and reduce numbness on long days.
- Sunglasses with a clear or yellow lens for dusk and rain.

## 2. Clothing

Plan for the weather of the route, not the current forecast. Pack for the coldest morning and the wettest afternoon.

- Riding shorts, 3 pairs. Padded shorts reduce saddle sores. A second pair lets you wash one each evening.
- Riding jerseys or tops, 3 pieces. Wicking fabric dries overnight and keeps you cooler.
- Base layer, 1 long sleeve. Adds warmth on cold mornings without bulk.
- Warm layer, such as a fleece or light insulated jacket. Needed for rest stops and descents.
- Waterproof rain jacket. Keeps wind and rain off on long wet days.
- Rain pants or leg covers. Keep your legs warm and dry, which matters more than most people expect.
- Socks, 5 pairs of cycling socks. One pair per riding day plus one spare. Wool dries well.
- Off-bike clothes, 2 sets: a t-shirt, shorts or trousers, and underwear. Keep these dry in a separate bag so you have something clean for dinner.
- Sleepwear and a warm hat or beanie. Evenings and mornings can be cold, even in summer.
- Cycling cap or buff. Keeps sweat out of your eyes and protects your neck.
- Sandals or light shoes for off the bike. Give your feet a break from cleats.
- Cycling shoes, worn on the flight if they are bulky. Check that they clear airport security.

## 3. Sleep and camp (if you camp or stay in hostels)

- Tent or hostel bed linen. Confirm reservations before you leave.
- Sleeping bag rated for the lowest expected temperature. Pack it in a compression sack to save space.
- Sleeping mat. Insulates you from cold ground and adds comfort.
- Pillow or inflatable neck pillow. Small weight, large gain in sleep quality.
- Headlamp with spare batteries. Hands-free light for camp chores and night toilet trips.

## 4. Toiletries and health

- Sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF. Riders get burned fast on long days.
- Chamois cream. Reduces friction and chafing on the saddle.
- Anti-chafe balm for other skin contact points.
- Pain relief, such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen. Keep it with you, not in checked luggage.
- Plasters or bandages, antiseptic wipes, and blister care items.
- Any prescription medication in the original labeled container, with a copy of the prescription.
- Personal toiletries in containers under 100 ml (3.4 oz) if you fly with carry-on liquids.
- Insect repellent. Needed in wooded or wet areas.
- Quick-dry towel. Lightweight and dries overnight.

## 5. Electronics and documents

- Phone with a waterproof case or bag. Your map, navigation, and emergency contact.
- Phone charger and a power bank of at least 10,000 mAh. Navigation and lights drain batteries quickly.
- Charging cables for all devices.
- Offline maps saved to your phone before the trip. Cell service often drops in rural areas.
- Passport or ID, travel insurance card, and emergency contacts on paper.
- Cash in small notes for small towns and villages that do not take cards.
- Bank card, with a second card stored separately.
- Written list of the route, stops, and booking references. Your phone may fail or lose power.

## 6. Repair and maintenance kit (in addition to Section 1)

- Small cloth and degreaser wipes. Keep the drivetrain clean and the chain lube working.
- Zip ties and duct tape wrapped around a water bottle. Fix broken racks, bags, and lights.
- Spare brake pads if your bike uses a standard pattern. Worn pads can fail on a long descent.
- Spare brake and gear cable, with the housing ends capped. Cables stretch and snap on long trips.
- Spare bolts or a few shim washers that fit your bike. Helpful for rack or fender repairs.

## 7. Packing and organization

- Pannier bags or a rack-top bag. Keep heavy items low and close to the bike center line.
- Dry bags or stuff sacks inside the panniers. Protect clothing and electronics from rain.
- Small bag for daily essentials on the handlebar or top tube. Keep it within reach at stops.
- Luggage tags with your name and contact details, on both your bag and the bike box.

## 8. Flying with the bike

- Remove pedals, turn the handlebars parallel to the frame, and deflate the tires to the minimum recommended level. Check your airline rules on bike boxes and fees.
- Wrap the frame in bubble wrap or a padded cover. Protect the derailleur and disc rotors.
- Carry the pedals, tools, and any loose parts inside the bike box, and mark the box clearly.
- Pack the chain lube, pump, and tools in carry-on only if the airline allows it. Sharp tools and some lubricants are restricted.

## Checklist before you leave

1. Weigh all bags and confirm they meet the airline limit.
2. Test ride the loaded bike for at least 20 minutes.
3. Check brakes, gears, tire pressure, and bolt torque.
4. Confirm lodging, route, and emergency contacts are saved offline.
5. Charge all devices and the power bank.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

This guide lists what to pack for a seven-day bike tour, with the reason for each item. Pack the bike-specific gear first, then clothing, then the rest. Weigh your loaded panniers before you leave, and aim to keep the total luggage near 15 kg (about 33 lb) or less.

## 1. Bike and safety

- Helmet. Protects your head in a fall or collision. Replace it if it has taken a hard hit.
- Lights, front and rear, plus spare batteries or a USB charger. Tours often include early starts, late arrivals, and tunnels or shaded roads.
- Bike lock with key or code. Needed for stops in towns, cafes, and campsites.
- Water bottles or a hydration bladder, two or more. Carry at least 1 liter per hour of riding in warm weather.
- Saddle bag or top tube bag with a multi-tool, tire levers, and a spare tube or two. Flats are the most common roadside problem.
- Tire pump or CO2 inflator with a spare cartridge. Confirm the valve type on your tires (Presta or Schrader) so the pump fits.
- Patch kit and spare spoke or derailleur hanger if your bike uses one. A bent hanger can end a trip, so carry the spare in your bag.
- Chain lube in a small bottle. Dry or dirty chains wear fast and skip under load.
- Chain tool, quick links, and a cassette or freewheel tool if your bike needs one.
- Reflective strips or a vest for riding in traffic or at dusk.
- Bike gloves. Protect your hands in a fall and reduce numbness on long days.
- Sunglasses with a clear or yellow lens for dusk and rain.

## 2. Clothing

Plan for the weather of the route, not the current forecast. Pack for the coldest morning and the wettest afternoon.

- Riding shorts, 3 pairs. Padded shorts reduce saddle sores. A second pair lets you wash one each evening.
- Riding jerseys or tops, 3 pieces. Wicking fabric dries overnight and keeps you cooler.
- Base layer, 1 long sleeve. Adds warmth on cold mornings without bulk.
- Warm layer, such as a fleece or light insulated jacket. Needed for rest stops and descents.
- Waterproof rain jacket. Keeps wind and rain off on long wet days.
- Rain pants or leg covers. Keep your legs warm and dry, which matters more than most people expect.
- Socks, 5 pairs of cycling socks. One pair per riding day plus one spare. Wool dries well.
- Off-bike clothes, 2 sets: a t-shirt, shorts or trousers, and underwear. Keep these dry in a separate bag so you have something clean for dinner.
- Sleepwear and a warm hat or beanie. Evenings and mornings can be cold, even in summer.
- Cycling cap or buff. Keeps sweat out of your eyes and protects your neck.
- Sandals or light shoes for off the bike. Give your feet a break from cleats.
- Cycling shoes, worn on the flight if they are bulky. Check that they clear airport security.

## 3. Sleep and camp (if you camp or stay in hostels)

- Tent or hostel bed linen. Confirm reservations before you leave.
- Sleeping bag rated for the lowest expected temperature. Pack it in a compression sack to save space.
- Sleeping mat. Insulates you from cold ground and adds comfort.
- Pillow or inflatable neck pillow. Small weight, large gain in sleep quality.
- Headlamp with spare batteries. Hands-free light for camp chores and night toilet trips.

## 4. Toiletries and health

- Sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, and lip balm with SPF. Riders get burned fast on long days.
- Chamois cream. Reduces friction and chafing on the saddle.
- Anti-chafe balm for other skin contact points.
- Pain relief, such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen. Keep it with you, not in checked luggage.
- Plasters or bandages, antiseptic wipes, and blister care items.
- Any prescription medication in the original labeled container, with a copy of the prescription.
- Personal toiletries in containers under 100 ml (3.4 oz) if you fly with carry-on liquids.
- Insect repellent. Needed in wooded or wet areas.
- Quick-dry towel. Lightweight and dries overnight.

## 5. Electronics and documents

- Phone with a waterproof case or bag. Your map, navigation, and emergency contact.
- Phone charger and a power bank of at least 10,000 mAh. Navigation and lights drain batteries quickly.
- Charging cables for all devices.
- Offline maps saved to your phone before the trip. Cell service often drops in rural areas.

- Dry bags or stuff sacks inside the panniers. Protect clothing and electronics from rain.
- Small bag for daily essentials on the handlebar or top tube. Keep it within reach at stops.

## 8. Flying with the bike

- Remove pedals, turn the handlebars parallel to the frame, and deflate the tires to the minimum recommended level. Check your airline rules on bike boxes and fees.
- Wrap the frame in bubble wrap or a padded cover. Protect the derailleur and disc rotors.
- Carry the pedals, tools, and any loose parts inside the bike box, and mark the box clearly.
- Pack the chain lube, pump, and tools in carry-on only if the airline allows it. Sharp tools and some lubricants are restricted.
